title: Continuous atomic-resolution crystallography inside working devices and static extreme environments

concept.text: Proposed innovation: determine independently validated atomic structures of crystalline working material repeatedly while it remains inside an operating device, or inside a static cell at extreme pressure and temperature. Examples include an electrode during battery cycling, a catalyst during reactor operation, and a mineral along a pressure–temperature path. The goal is to refine the positions and other supported structural properties of atoms under the conditions being studied, rather than obtain only lattice parameters, phase fractions or strain maps.

Scope definition: operating devices and static extreme-environment cells are two distinct demonstration settings, with different requirements for access, sampled volume, timing and validation. Here, continuous means sustained structure determination at a defined cadence sufficient to resolve the structural changes of interest. Several isolated structures would demonstrate repeated in situ measurement, but would not alone establish that capability. The target concerns the crystalline material actually present in the device or cell; it does not automatically encompass every grain, amorphous component or interface.

significance.text: Conditional significance: achieving this capability would connect validated atomic models directly to operating conditions. Researchers could compare the structures present during charging, catalysis or a pressure–temperature change with the behavior measured at the same time. This could reveal structural states that disappear during removal, relaxation or quenching, provided the measurements have sufficient temporal resolution, spatial coverage and sensitivity.

Scientific distinction: conventional single-crystal model completeness does not guarantee complete characterization of disorder or defects. An atomic model can describe an average structure while missing rare defects, heterogeneous local arrangements or rapidly changing populations. Resolving those features would require appropriate measurements and validation beyond a count of modeled atoms. Likewise, repeated structures would not by themselves constitute movies of elementary chemical steps.

Conditional downstream possibilities: the resulting structures could constrain models of electrode degradation, catalytic activity and minerals under extreme conditions. Predicting battery performance, reaction rates or planetary behavior would still require transport, kinetics, electrochemistry and other relevant information. Structural access would supply an important experimental foundation rather than a complete predictive model.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed missing capability: sustain enough structural information and independent validation to refine atomic models of the working crystalline material throughout a defined operating cycle or pressure–temperature path. The central challenge is to combine atomic structural completeness with access to the actual sample, adequate time resolution and sufficiently limited measurement disturbance. The supplied evidence does not establish how broadly this capability is currently absent, so the claim that it remains open across the entire proposed scope requires further documentation.

Engineering synthesis: candidate obstacles in devices include attenuation and background from packaging, overlapping signals from multiple phases or grains, spatial heterogeneity, and changes occurring while diffraction data are collected. A successful method would need to identify which material and volume each model represents, collect enough independent information within the relevant time window, and determine whether irradiation changes the operating behavior. These are system-dependent challenges, not documented properties of every working device.

Engineering synthesis: static extreme-environment cells present a different combination of potential barriers, including restricted angular access, small crystals, cell background, pressure gradients, departures from hydrostatic conditions and temperature gradients. Combined pressure and temperature also complicate sample stability, calibration and structural refinement. Their severity must be established for each proposed apparatus. The supplied material does not justify a feasibility ranking for unmodified commercial devices versus multi-megabar, high-temperature chambers.

The retained protein-cell abstract provides a limited experimental foundation for pressure-dependent atomic crystallography: it reports helium pressurization up to 120 MPa in one sapphire-capillary apparatus. That range is a demonstrated capability of the reported cell, not a field-wide upper limit for macromolecular crystallography or evidence of performance at combined extreme pressure and temperature.

current_state.text: The retained PubMed record identifies a Lieske and co-authors IUCrJ article dated 1 November 2026, DOI 10.1107/S2052252526008468. Its abstract reports a sapphire-capillary macromolecular crystallography cell pressurized with helium up to 120 MPa and describes atomic-resolution structural investigation under pressure. Across five proteins, the authors generally observed structural compression and decreased thermal displacement parameters, together with additional conformational observations. This is a specific reported advance in protein crystallography under pressure; it does not demonstrate the full operating-device or combined extreme pressure–temperature capability proposed here.

The available evidence for that result consists of an abstract and bibliographic record, rather than the full article. The supplied review verified the article identity and the abstract's pressure range and five-protein observations. Detailed experimental validation, refinement quality, reproducibility and the breadth of the conformational findings cannot be assessed from the retained material. This access limitation restricts interpretation without establishing that the reported result is false.

The earlier research attributes operando synchrotron diffraction, reciprocal-space mapping and Bragg coherent diffraction imaging of battery materials to a Chemical Reviews article identified as published online on 3 October 2025. It describes investigations of strain, cation disorder, phase transitions and defects. However, no source text or retained artifact accompanies that citation, so its identity, date and exact technical scope remain unverified in the supplied review. This attribution cannot establish either routine full atomic structure determination in working electrodes or its general absence.

Evidence synthesis: the supplied material supports the dated protein-cell report but does not establish the broader frontier of operando atomic structure determination or static high-pressure crystallography. The earlier research also invokes CRX-08 for existing static structures and dynamic diffraction, but no underlying evidence from that entry is supplied. The bounded search record is empty, so freshness and the present-day openness of the full target remain unassessed. No supplied result demonstrates sustained, independently validated atomic completeness across either full demonstration setting.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: obtain and refine atomic models during operation of a battery or catalytic reactor, and separately inside a static high-pressure, high-temperature cell. In each setting, the measured material must remain inside the device or cell under the conditions claimed. Pre-register material-appropriate ex situ single-crystal benchmarks for non-hydrogen structural completeness and independent validation, then show that the in situ models meet those benchmarks. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Atomic models meet benchmarks in operating devices and extreme cells

completion_criteria.text: Proposed temporal and spatial requirements: specify the sampled volume, material identity, exposure and acquisition time, reconstruction or refinement latency, and interval between validated models. Measure several points through an operating cycle or pressure–temperature path to establish repeated structure determination. To substantiate the title's continuous capability, additionally demonstrate a pre-registered cadence that resolves the structural changes of interest over a declared duration, and report gaps or failed refinements.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated validated models resolve structural changes at a pre-registered cadence

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation and reproducibility: use independent structural checks appropriate to the material, report uncertainty and alternative interpretations, and test whether the measurement perturbs device operation or sample state. Repeat the demonstration on independent samples or cycles, with sufficient methods and data for independent reproduction. Lattice parameters alone, a strain map, phase fractions, or a single structure obtained after quenching would not satisfy the proposed atomic-model benchmark.
completion_criteria.label: Independently validated atomic models are reproducible across samples or cycles

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report the demonstrated pressure and temperature ranges, device modifications, packaging, crystal size, material classes, dose and usable acquisition cadence. State separately whether disorder, defects, interfaces, minor phases or hydrogen positions are resolved. Success in a purpose-built cell would establish capability in that geometry; claims about unmodified commercial devices would require corresponding demonstrations. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Report demonstrated experimental scope and limits of structural resolution

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: CRX-06, Atomic movies of elementary chemical steps without a photo-trigger, overlaps in observing structural change over time. CRX-12 instead emphasizes sustained atomic structure determination inside operating devices and static extreme environments; its cadence need not resolve elementary reaction steps. CRX-08, Ab initio atomic structure of matter that exists only once, addresses one-time structural access, whereas CRX-12 requires repeated access to material maintained under the conditions of interest. These distinctions follow from the supplied titles and research descriptions; detailed records for CRX-06 and CRX-08 are unavailable.

Roster-based distinction: CRX-01 concerns a single non-crystalline molecule before destruction, and CRX-02 concerns chemically complete structures of bulk amorphous solids. CRX-12 retains a crystalline structural target within a challenging environment. CRX-04, Atomic ensembles measured from total X-ray scattering, could provide complementary information about distributions and disorder that a conventional refined crystal model may not capture. Its ensemble objective remains distinct from sustained in-device crystallographic refinement.

Roster-based distinction: CRX-05 seeks experimental many-electron quantum states, while CRX-09 seeks routine crystallographic protonation-state assignment. Both extend the information obtainable from structural experiments. CRX-12 primarily changes where and over what duration validated atomic structures can be measured; its proposed non-hydrogen completeness benchmark would not automatically deliver either electronic quantum states or protonation states.

Roster-based distinction: CRX-03 predicts which molecular crystal will form, CRX-07 seeks experimental selection of a chosen crystal form, and CRX-13 seeks growth rules that suppress defects, twins and disorder. They concern formation or control of crystalline material. CRX-12 concerns observing material under working conditions and could supply useful structural observations for those efforts, without itself predicting or controlling crystallization.

Roster-based distinction: CRX-10 seeks laboratory sources capable of facility-class coherent X-ray crystallography, and CRX-11 seeks diffraction-quality crystals of arbitrary macromolecules on demand. Better sources or sample preparation could help some CRX-12 implementations. Neither alone resolves access through a device or extreme-environment cell, time-dependent data acquisition, or independent validation under the claimed conditions.

unresolved_issues: The current breadth and routine availability of independently validated atomic models inside operating devices and combined extreme pressure–temperature cells are not established by the supplied evidence.
The cited Chemical Reviews article's identity, publication date and technical claims remain unverified because no retained source text is available.
The protein-cell report is available only through its abstract and bibliographic record; detailed refinement quality, reproducibility and experimental limitations remain unassessed.
Suitable material-specific completeness benchmarks, independent validation methods, acquisition cadence and observation duration remain to be defined for each demonstration.
Performance in unmodified commercial devices or multi-megabar, high-temperature chambers remains unestablished; the supplied evidence does not support a feasibility ranking.
The extent to which the proposed measurements could resolve disorder, defects or transient structures lost on quenching remains dependent on spatial coverage, sensitivity and timing.
Detailed overlap with neighboring concepts, especially CRX-06 and CRX-08, cannot be fully assessed from roster titles and brief research descriptions.
Freshness remains unassessed because the supplied bounded search record is empty.

brief.title: Atomic structures tracked inside working devices
possible: Researchers could track where atoms sit in crystalline materials—solids with repeating atomic patterns—while a battery charges or a reactor runs. They could also follow those structures inside a cell holding a sample under extreme pressure and temperature, without removing it.
why: Matching atomic structures to behavior measured at the same time could help explain battery degradation, catalytic activity and mineral behavior under extreme conditions.
Structures that disappear when a sample is removed or cooled could become accessible. Researchers could use them to build better models of how materials behave.

sources.showed: This is a review of studies using X-ray scattering to investigate battery materials during operation.
sources.cited_for: It provides background on studies of structural changes in working battery materials.
sources.not_established: Such studies do not by themselves establish sustained, independently validated atomic structures inside working electrodes.

sources.showed: They built a helium-pressurized sapphire tube for determining protein structures with X-rays. They observed compressed protein structures and less variation in atomic positions under pressure.
sources.quote: Studying five different proteins, we generally observed a compression of the protein structures and a decrease in thermal displacement parameters at high pressure.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates atomic structural measurements of proteins under pressure.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate sustained atomic structure tracking inside working devices or under combined extreme pressure and temperature.

shown: Julia Lieske and collaborators built a protein crystallography cell, which uses X-rays to determine atomic arrangements, reaching pressures of 120 MPa. They observed compression and changes in protein shape under pressure.
missing: Atomic models would have to meet independent checks while the material remains inside a working device and, separately, a hot, high-pressure cell.
Measurements would have to sustain a pace that resolves the relevant structural changes throughout an operating cycle or pressure–temperature path.
Repeated trials would have to establish reproducibility and whether the measurements themselves change the material or device behavior.

milestones.label: Atomic models meet benchmarks in both settings
milestones.explanation: Models in working devices and, separately, hot, high-pressure cells would have to meet advance benchmarks for completeness excluding hydrogen and independent checks. This would establish atomic detail under the claimed conditions.

milestones.label: Validated models keep pace with structural changes
milestones.explanation: Repeated, checked models would have to resolve changes at a pace and duration set in advance, with sampled material and measurement gaps identified. This would establish sustained tracking.

milestones.label: Independent checks and repeated trials confirm the models
milestones.explanation: Independent checks and repeat samples or cycles would have to confirm the models, quantify uncertainty and test measurement disturbance. This would establish that the structures reliably represent the material being studied.

milestones.label: Experiments establish the capability’s reach and limits
milestones.explanation: Experiments would have to report operating ranges, apparatus changes, materials, measurement exposure and pace, and which structural features they resolve. This would define where the capability works.

uncertain: How widely sustained, independently checked atomic structure determination already works across these settings remains unclear.
Suitable completeness benchmarks, independent checks and measurement timing depend on the material and the changes being studied.
An average atomic structure may miss rare defects, interfaces or short-lived arrangements; resolving them depends on coverage, sensitivity and timing.
